claims.text: The relevant material family is Fe-Co-Ni-based fcc high-entropy alloys, including CoCrFeMnNi.
The intrinsic stacking-fault energy exhibits non-monotonic temperature dependence below 430 K.
The cryogenic temperature dependence of stacking-fault energy is caused by an interplay between longitudinal spin fluctuations and magneto-volume coupling.
The initial material is an equiatomic, fcc, Fe-Co-Ni-based alloy such as CoCrFeMnNi.
The alloy is in a paramagnetic state at cryogenic temperatures of 50–300 K.
Conventional static calculations give zero magnetic moments for Cr and Ni.
The relevant calculations cover 50–430 K under ambient pressure represented using experimental thermal expansion.
The material remains fcc-dominant but may nucleate hcp at low temperatures.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce finite local magnetic moments on Co, Cr, and Ni.
The induced local moments and magneto-volume coupling alter the internal-energy and magnetic-entropy contributions to stacking-fault energy.
Magnetic entropy from the fluctuation-induced moments, together with magneto-volume coupling, drives the temperature dependence of stacking-fault energy.
Standard DFT-LSDA/GGA treatments often neglect the orbital component of the magnetic moment.
The orbital-moment component significantly affects magnetic entropy and consequently shifts the fcc-hcp transition temperature and the sign of the stacking-fault energy.
Enhancing orbital moments will increase magnetic entropy and raise cryogenic intrinsic stacking-fault energy relative to calculations that ignore orbital moments.
Raising the cryogenic stacking-fault energy may suppress experimentally observed nano-twins and stacking faults.
DLM-LSF calculations predict an intrinsic stacking-fault energy of approximately -17 mJ m^-2 at 50 K.
DLM-LSF calculations predict an fcc-hcp transition temperature of approximately 430 K, compared with an experimental value of approximately 633 K.
Neglected phonon effects may explain the discrepancy between the predicted and experimental transition temperatures.
The cited evidence does not quantify the orbital-moment contribution to magnetic entropy.
